A B-tree index helps a database find rows without scanning an entire table. It organizes sorted keys into a balanced tree of pages, each holding many keys and pointers.

A lookup starts at the root page. The database compares the requested key with separator keys, then follows a pointer to the child covering the appropriate range. It repeats this process until reaching a leaf, where entries identify matching rows or contain the rows themselves, depending on the implementation.

Because each page has many children and all leaves are at the same depth, the tree stays shallow. Even a large index typically needs only a few page reads per lookup.

For range queries, the database finds the first matching key and scans entries in sorted order. This ordering can also help satisfy `ORDER BY`.

Inserts and deletes maintain balance through operations such as page splits and merges, adding storage and write overhead.
